results.result: The manuscript establishes the general problem that nonlinear circuit components in neural systems are difficult to isolate and study, particularly in the context of photoreceptor processing where linear models fail to capture spatially local adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C10, C14, and C128 collectively establish the scientific motivation for the work through citations to prior literature and logical reasoning about the limitations of current approaches. These are well-supported background claims that frame the problem addressed by the manuscript.

results.result: The authors introduce a tool based on phototransduction models that permits the design of light stimuli to predictably alter rod and cone responses, compensate for nonlinear properties like adaptation, and separate phototransduction nonlinearities from downstream circuit nonlinearities.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 describe the main contribution of the paper. The tool is demonstrated experimentally throughout Figures 6-10, showing successful manipulation of photoreceptor responses. The ability to separate phototransduction from downstream nonlinearities is validated in Figure 10. This is the central result of the manuscript.

results.result: Existing biochemical phototransduction models with appropriate parameters (4 free parameters for rods, 5 for cones) can account for responses of rod and cone photoreceptors from both primate and mouse to a broad range of inputs, capturing >80% of response variance on average.
results.evaluation: Claims C15 and C40-C49, C54 are supported by extensive experimental validation in Figures 1-2 and supplementary figures. The models generalize well across stimuli and cells, with parameters well-constrained by the data (10-20% changes significantly increase MSE). Consensus models perform similarly to individually-fitted models, demonstrating robustness.

results.result: The biochemical model architecture was chosen for its mechanistic connection to phototransduction and exact invertibility, with 11 total parameters reduced to 4-5 free parameters through constraints based on steady-state conditions and prior measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C26-C34 describe the model structure and parameter reduction strategy. The choices are justified by citations to prior work and mathematical constraints. The resulting parameter set is shown to be well-constrained by the data (C41-C42), supporting the validity of these methodological decisions.

results.result: Rod photoreceptors were recorded using suction electrodes allowing comprehensive stimulus testing from individual cells, while cone photoreceptors were recorded using whole-cell patch clamp with shorter stable recording periods, limiting data collection to single stimulus types per cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 describe the experimental methods and their constraints. These are straightforward methodological descriptions consistent with standard electrophysiological practices and the data presented in the figures.

results.result: Linear models of phototransduction deviate considerably more from measured responses than biochemical models, specifically overpredicting responses at high mean light levels and underpredicting at low mean light levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, which quantitatively compare linear and biochemical model performance. The linear model captures ~60-85% of variance compared to ~90% for the biochemical model, demonstrating the importance of capturing nonlinearities.

results.result: The phototransduction model can be exactly mathematically inverted to identify stimuli corresponding to desired photoreceptor responses, with the inversion procedure exactly recovering test stimuli used to generate model currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C63 describe the mathematical invertibility of the model and demonstrate it in Figure 3. The model consists of invertible components (linear filters, static nonlinearities, and an analytically solvable time-dependent nonlinearity), and the inversion exactly recovers the test stimulus, confirming mathematical correctness.

results.result: Stimulus estimates based on measured photoreceptor responses closely approximate actual stimuli, capturing the majority of stimulus variance, with accuracy depending on temporal frequency (convergence at ~30 Hz for primate cones, ~10 Hz for mouse cones, ~2-3 Hz for rods).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71 are supported by Figures 4-5, which show quantitative validation of stimulus estimation from measured responses. The frequency-dependent accuracy is clearly demonstrated in power spectra (Figure 5), and the constraints applied (frequency limits, power spectrum matching) are appropriate for dealing with noise in deconvolution.

results.result: Adaptive nonlinearities in phototransduction cause strongly nonsinusoidal responses to sinusoidal light inputs, with asymmetries between increments/decrements and light-to-dark/dark-to-light transitions that can be substantially reduced using model-designed modified stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 are validated in Figures 6-7. The nonsinusoidal responses to sinusoidal stimuli are clearly demonstrated, and modified stimuli produce significantly more sinusoidal responses (lower MSE) across all photoreceptor types tested. Importantly, the test cells and stimuli were independent of model fitting (C80), demonstrating generalization.

results.result: Modified stimuli designed using model inversion can compensate for adaptive gain changes produced by changes in mean light intensity, reducing the ~twofold decrease in flash response amplitude at higher backgrounds across all photoreceptor types.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by Figure 8, which shows that modified stimuli substantially reduce adaptation-induced gain changes. The validation uses independent test cells (C85), and the effect is consistent across primate and mouse rods and cones, though some systematic differences suggest cell-to-cell variability.

results.result: Model inversion can predictably alter photoreceptor response kinetics, slowing responses substantially and speeding responses by 20-30%, with measured time-to-peak changes closely following predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are validated in Figure 9, which shows successful manipulation of response kinetics in both directions. The measured time-to-peak changes closely match predictions (Figure 9C), though speeding is more limited than slowing due to physical constraints on light intensities.

results.result: Modified stimuli that negate cone adaptation eliminate most adaptation in downstream horizontal cells and On parasol ganglion cells, while revealing additional time-independent nonlinearities in horizontal and bipolar cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by Figure 10, which demonstrates that compensating for cone adaptation eliminates downstream adaptation (Figure 10A-B) and reveals additional nonlinear processes (Figure 10C-D). This validates the tool's ability to separate phototransduction from post-transduction nonlinearities, a key application of the approach.

results.result: The model inversion procedure's accuracy depends on model quality, with validation showing relatively small systematic differences between predicted and measured responses that mostly reflect cell-to-cell variability rather than model failures.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 acknowledge limitations and describe the validation strategy. The extensive testing on independent cells and stimuli (Figures 6-9) supports the conclusion that differences are primarily due to biological variability rather than systematic model errors.

results.result: The model is limited to phototransduction currents (not synaptic output) and does not include photopigment bleaching, restricting cone models to light levels <50,000 R*/s while covering most of the rod operating range.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C104 clearly describe the scope and limitations of the model. These limitations are justified by experimental constraints (removal of pigment epithelium) and the operating ranges of rods vs. cones. The authors appropriately acknowledge these boundaries.

results.result: Speeding responses is limited by the requirement for non-negative light intensities, meaning low-contrast stimuli can be sped more than high-contrast stimuli, and accurate light calibrations are critical for model predictions to translate across laboratories.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 describe practical limitations and requirements. The constraint on speeding is a logical consequence of physics (C106) and is demonstrated in the data (Figure 9). The importance of calibration (C108) is a standard requirement for quantitative experiments.

results.result: The photoreceptor models can serve as a front end for encoding models of downstream responses, capturing time-dependent nonlinearities that are difficult for empirical and CNN models, with hybrid models showing improved performance in predicting retinal ganglion cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 describe an application of the models. Claims C110-C112 about limitations of existing models are supported by general knowledge. Claim C115 is supported by citation to recent work (Idrees et al., 2024), while C114 is a reasonable prediction based on the demonstrated capabilities.

results.result: Incorporating the inverse photoreceptor model into decoding approaches should improve decoding performance by separating photoreceptor adaptation from downstream processing.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is a prediction about a potential application that has not been tested in this manuscript. While the logic is sound given the demonstrated capabilities, this remains speculative without experimental validation.

results.result: The stimulus design approach complements genetic manipulations by allowing specific functional manipulations without requiring genetic access, though providing less detailed mechanistic information than genetic approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 compare the approach to genetic methods. C117-C118 are supported by citations to genetic studies and their known limitations. C119-C120 are reasonable assessments of the relative strengths and weaknesses of the two approaches, though C119 is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The tool enables testing whether On/Off asymmetries in visual processing originate from asymmetric photoreceptor responses to increments and decrements, challenging the common assumption that photoreceptor inputs to On and Off circuits are symmetrical for high-contrast stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C127 describe an important application. C121-C125 are supported by citations and logical reasoning about photoreceptor adaptation. C126 is supported by citation to work using this approach (Yu et al., 2022). C127 summarizes the general utility, which is demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

results.result: A key feature of the photoreceptor models is their ability to generalize across stimuli, including accounting for nonlinear properties of responses to stimuli not used in model fitting.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 is validated throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 (supplement 1), 7-9, where models trained on one set of stimuli successfully predict responses to different stimuli and in different cells. This generalization is essential for the tool's utility.

results.result: Current models for retinal processing assume linear or near-linear photoreceptor responses despite evidence to the contrary, and both photoreceptors and post-photoreceptor circuits adapt to prevailing light inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 describe the state of the field and are supported by citations to review articles and specific modeling approaches. These establish the motivation for developing better tools to account for photoreceptor nonlinearities.

results.result: The phototransduction cascade operates through well-established mechanisms involving cGMP-gated channels, G-protein coupled receptors, phosphodiesterase, guanylate cyclase, and calcium feedback that strongly shapes light responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 describe established knowledge about phototransduction supported by citations to review articles and primary literature. These provide the biological foundation for the biochemical model used in the study.

results.result: The authors developed an invertible computational tool based on phototransduction models that can design light stimuli to predictably alter rod and cone photocurrents, including compensating for nonlinear properties like light adaptation. This tool permits separation of phototransduction nonlinearities from downstream circuit nonlinearities.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core contribution. Reviewer 1 states the paper 'provides an important method' and 'compelling evidence that this approach can disentangle the effects of photoreceptor nonlinearities.' Reviewer 2 calls the approach 'impressive' and 'convincing,' noting it 'should be a powerful tool for future investigations.' Reviewer 3 describes the approach as 'simple and elegant' with data that 'support the authors conclusions.'

results.result: Existing phototransduction models with optimized parameters (4 free parameters for rods, 5 for cones) accurately capture photoreceptor responses across diverse stimuli in both mouse and primate. Consensus models captured >80% of response variance for individual cells and ~90% on average, generalizing well across stimuli and to held-out cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently praise the model's performance. Reviewer 2 states 'the ability to capture responses to stimuli as different as white noise with varying mean intensity and flashes with a common set of model parameters across cells is impressive' and notes the presentation is 'thorough and convincing.' Reviewer 3 describes the recordings as 'impressive.' The only noted weakness is that the model is 'not perfect, including some small systematic differences' (Reviewer 2), which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: The phototransduction model can be mathematically inverted because it consists of invertible linear elements, static nonlinear elements, and a time-dependent nonlinear element. The inversion procedure exactly recovers stimuli used to generate test currents, producing estimates in real units (isomerizations per second).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mathematical invertibility without challenge. Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'the biophysical modeling approach is well described.' Reviewer 2 appreciates 'the clear exposition' that facilitates application by other labs. No reviewer questions the mathematical validity of the inversion procedure.

results.result: Stimulus estimates based on model inversion from measured photoreceptor responses closely approximate actual stimuli, capturing the majority of stimulus variance and accurately recovering rapid fluctuations at low temporal frequencies (up to ~30 Hz for primate cones, ~10 Hz for mouse cones, ~2-3 Hz for rods).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these validation results. Reviewer 2 notes the examples of model application are 'convincing' and that models 'generalized well across stimuli.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors demonstrate through additional experiments that their proposed approach works.' The frequency-dependent performance is presented as data without reviewer objection.

results.result: Modified stimuli designed via model inversion successfully linearize photoreceptor responses to sinusoidal inputs. Responses to modified stimuli were much closer to sinusoidal than responses to original sinusoidal stimuli, with substantially reduced asymmetries between increments/decrements and faster/slower transitions, as quantified by lower MSE in sinusoidal fits.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these results without criticism. Reviewer 2 describes the examples as 'convincing' and notes they 'corroborate, for example, previous findings that adaptation to ambient light in the primate retina...mostly originates in photoreceptors.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the authors demonstrate through additional experiments that their proposed approach works and is useful for offering insights into retinal computation.'

results.result: Modified stimuli designed to compensate for photoreceptor adaptation successfully reduced gain changes produced by background light. For control stimuli, flash responses decreased ~twofold at higher mean light levels, but modified stimuli produced similar flash response amplitudes at low and high mean light levels across all photoreceptor types tested on held-out cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these adaptation compensation results. Reviewer 1 specifically mentions the approach can 'disentangle the effects of photoreceptor nonlinearities including light adaptation from downstream nonlinear processing.' Reviewer 2 notes the examples 'corroborate...previous findings that adaptation to ambient light in the primate retina...mostly originates in photoreceptors.' No concerns are raised about these experimental demonstrations.

results.result: Model inversion can predictably alter response kinetics, slowing or speeding photoreceptor responses. Speeding responses by 20-30% is achievable, and measured time-to-peak changes closely follow model predictions for both slowing and speeding manipulations in rods and cones.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these kinetic manipulation results. Reviewer 2 describes the approach as allowing manipulation of 'visual stimuli in such a way that photoreceptor signals are linear or have reduced or altered adaptation,' implicitly including kinetic alterations. Reviewer 3 notes the approach 'works' based on additional experiments. The quantitative agreement between predictions and measurements is presented without reviewer objection.

results.result: Modified stimuli that negate cone adaptation effectively eliminated most adaptation in downstream horizontal cells and On parasol ganglion cells. Compensating for phototransduction nonlinearities revealed additional, largely time-independent nonlinear processes in horizontal and bipolar cell responses, demonstrating the approach can disentangle contributions of phototransduction versus post-transduction processes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this application. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide compelling evidence that this approach can disentangle the effects of photoreceptor nonlinearities including light adaptation from downstream nonlinear processing, thus facilitating future studies of the higher visual system.' Reviewer 2 calls this 'thought-provoking' and notes it 'should be a powerful tool for future investigations of retinal circuit function.' Reviewer 3 confirms the approach is 'useful for offering insights into retinal computation.'

results.result: The model's accuracy depends on its quality, but systematic differences between predicted and measured responses were relatively small when consensus models were tested on held-out cells from different retinas. Most differences appear to reflect cell-to-cell variability rather than systematic model failures.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes this as a weakness: 'The model is impressive, but not perfect, including some small systematic differences between model predictions and measurements from held-out cells. The deviations likely (partly) reflect differences between cells used for parameter optimization and test cells, as stated in the text (though this is not fully proven), which has to be kept in mind when applying the model.' This indicates the generalization is good but imperfect, with uncertainty about the source of remaining errors.

results.result: The model describes photocurrents rather than synaptic output and does not include photopigment bleaching/regeneration. It is limited to light levels <50,000 R*/s for cones (though covers most of the rod operating range), as experiments required pigment epithelium removal and minimized bleaching.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these limitations without criticism. Reviewer 2 states: 'The model is limited to describing photoreceptor responses at the level of photocurrents, as opposed to the output of the cell, which takes into account voltage-dependent mechanisms, horizontal cell feedback, etc., as the authors acknowledge. It could be interesting to expand the model in the future to include factors that affect photoreceptor output beyond the stage of the photocurrent.' This is presented as a recognized scope limitation rather than a flaw.

results.result: A biochemical model architecture was chosen for its mechanistic connection to phototransduction and exact invertibility. The 11-parameter model was reduced to 4-5 free parameters through constraints and prior measurements, with parameters optimized separately for each photoreceptor type.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the modeling choices. Reviewer 3 specifically states 'the biophysical modeling approach is well described.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the presentation of the model is thorough and convincing' and appreciates 'the clear exposition and the listing of obtained optimal parameter values.' No reviewer questions the parameter reduction strategy or model architecture choice.

results.result: Rods were recorded with suction electrodes allowing comprehensive stimulus sets per cell, while cones were recorded with whole-cell patch clamp with shorter stability requiring single stimulus types per cell due to internal dialysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the experimental approach. Reviewer 3 states 'the authors collected an impressive set of recordings from mouse and primate photoreceptors, which is very challenging to obtain.' The methodological differences between rod and cone recordings are presented as technical constraints without reviewer criticism.

results.result: Linear models of photoreceptor responses deviated considerably more from measured responses than the biochemical model, specifically overpredicting responses at high mean light levels and underpredicting at low mean light levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this comparison. Reviewer 2 notes the model's ability to capture responses 'is impressive' compared to simpler alternatives. The superiority of the nonlinear biochemical model over linear approximations is presented as supporting evidence for the approach without reviewer objection.

results.result: Stimulus frequency content was limited to frequencies photoreceptors can encode (0-60 Hz primate cones, 0-30 Hz mouse cones, 0-15 Hz rods) and power spectra were matched to reduce noise amplification at high frequencies where photoreceptors poorly encode signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these methodological constraints without criticism. The frequency limitations are presented as reasonable technical considerations given photoreceptor encoding properties, and no reviewer questions this approach to managing noise in the inversion procedure.

results.result: Speeding responses is particularly difficult because it requires amplifying high temporal frequencies, and the ability to speed is limited by the physical constraint that light intensities cannot be negative. Low-contrast stimuli can be sped more than high-contrast stimuli.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these technical limitations. The constraints are presented as logical consequences of the physics of light stimulation and signal processing requirements. No reviewer questions why speeding is more limited than slowing or other kinetic manipulations.

results.result: Model prediction accuracy depends critically on accurate light calibrations, but with consistent calibrations the approach should translate directly across laboratories and to in vivo physiological or perceptual studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support generalizability. Reviewer 2 states 'Ideally, the present results would generalize to the work in other labs and possibly other sensory systems. The authors do provide evidence that a photocurrent model constructed from data in one set of cells can be used in a second set of cells.' Reviewer 3 notes the approach 'may be useful in vivo.' The calibration requirement is presented as a standard experimental consideration.

results.result: The photoreceptor models can serve as a front end for empirical models of downstream processing, potentially improving predictions of retinal responses across light levels and decoding performance. Hybrid models with phototransduction front ends show improved performance in predicting ganglion cell responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers view this positively. Reviewer 1 states the approach will facilitate 'future studies of the higher visual system.' Reviewer 2 calls it 'thought-provoking' and 'a powerful tool for future investigations of retinal circuit function.' The citation to improved hybrid model performance (Idrees et al., 2024) is presented without reviewer challenge.

results.result: The stimulus design approach could be used with genetic manipulations to restore normal kinetics or provides an alternative that allows specific functional manipulations without requiring genetic access. It permits testing how photoreceptor asymmetries contribute to On/Off differences in downstream responses and generally isolates photoreceptor versus post-photoreceptor circuit effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support these potential applications. Reviewer 1 emphasizes the approach 'can disentangle the effects of photoreceptor nonlinearities...from downstream nonlinear processing, thus facilitating future studies.' Reviewer 2 notes it addresses 'a long-standing problem in the field: determining the location of nonlinearities within a complex circuit.' Reviewer 3 confirms it is 'useful for offering insights into retinal computation.'
